name: Asset Management
description: Iranian asset management includes investment funds and portfolio-management services within the country's capital-market infrastructure. Historical institutional and company documents illustrate this ecosystem, but do not establish current product availability, licensing, or investment access.

seo.title: Asset Management in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian investment funds, portfolio management, and the evidence needed to understand digital asset-management services.

content.heading: A capital-market service
content.content:
Asset management belongs within a broader financial system rather than forming a single kind of technology company. A presentation by the research department of Iran's Securities and Exchange Organization, or SEO, distinguishes funds, portfolio managers, brokers, investment advisers, and investment companies. These categories help international readers understand why executing a securities trade, advising a client, and managing investments are different activities. The presentation describes investor protection and market supervision as part of the SEO's mandate; this is an institutional statement of responsibilities, not evidence that every investor receives effective protection. [s1]

The same document lists equity, balanced, fixed-income, market-making, private-equity, venture-capital, property, and project-oriented funds. It also distinguishes exchange-traded and open-ended structures. These labels describe different aspects of a product: its investment exposure and the way investors enter or leave it. They should not be treated as interchangeable categories or as proof of current availability. [s1]

content.heading: A documented example of product development
content.content:
An April 2017 presentation from Turquoise Partners provides a historical example of how an Iranian financial group combined investment management with brokerage and advisory services. Its chronology records the launch of an Iran equity fund, a domestic mutual fund, and an index-linked exchange-traded fund. These are the company's retrospective statements, rather than a verified inventory of products operating at the research cutoff. [s2]

The presentation also distinguishes a domestic fund reporting in Iranian rials from a foreign fund reporting in euros while holding rial-denominated assets. That distinction matters when interpreting performance: the reporting currency and the currency of the underlying investments are separate facts. A return figure without its currency, period, fee treatment, and exchange-rate methodology would provide an incomplete comparison. Historical promotional rankings in the document are therefore not reproduced here as present-day performance conclusions. [s2]

content.heading: Understanding the digital layer
content.content:
The historical Turquoise document describes online brokerage with live market information alongside managed accounts and portfolio services. This illustrates an important distinction for readers encountering financial applications: a digital interface can support several financial functions, but the interface alone does not identify the underlying service or its mandate. The document establishes a historical offering, not the functionality of a current application. [s2]

A current account of this sector needs dated regulatory records, product documents, and reproducible fund data. The inspected sources do not establish current fees, redemption conditions, provider authorizations, or cross-border eligibility. This page consequently offers a supported introduction rather than a provider ranking or an investment recommendation.

name: Insurance Technology
description: Insurance technology in Iran includes the software used to administer insurance operations, analyze business information, and connect digital services. Inspected Iranian vendor documentation demonstrates these functions, while leaving market-wide adoption and independently measured outcomes unresolved.

seo.title: Insurance Technology in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iranian insurance software, analytics, integration, and the distinction between advertised capabilities and verified outcomes.

content.heading: More than a place to buy insurance
content.content:
A useful introduction to Iranian insurance technology begins behind the customer interface. Fanavaran, an Iranian insurance-software supplier also using the name IranEIT, describes a product portfolio spanning core insurance administration, analytical reporting, digital health interactions, application programming interfaces, and reinsurance. An application programming interface, or API, allows software systems to exchange requests and information. Its presence in a supplier's portfolio demonstrates an integration offering; it does not establish unrestricted public access. [s1]

These functions explain why insurance technology cannot be assessed solely through the convenience of an online purchase. Policy administration records the insurance contract, claims systems handle reported losses, and analytical systems organize information for business decisions. The supplier's documentation supports this functional distinction, but does not independently demonstrate faster settlement, lower costs, or better customer outcomes. [s1]

content.heading: From operational records to analysis
content.content:
Fanavaran's Pooyan and Pooyesh documentation describes analytical databases, data transfer, management dashboards, and specialized insurance reports. It identifies Bonyan, the company's core insurance platform, as a source for reporting across operational subsystems. A data warehouse in this setting organizes operational information for analysis rather than replacing the insurance transaction system. [s2]

The product page also lists fraud detection. That is evidence of an advertised product component, not evidence of its accuracy. The inspected page supplies no independent evaluation of false alerts, missed cases, or financial savings. Readers should therefore distinguish the availability of an analytical tool from a demonstrated improvement in insurance decisions. [s2]

content.heading: Technology for sharing insurance risk
content.content:
Reinsurance is another part of the documented software landscape. Fanavaran separates business ceded to other insurers from business accepted from them, and lists software for several contractual arrangements. Its product page describes recording reinsurance operations, technical calculations, financial processing, reports, and access controls. It also states that the reinsurance solution can operate independently of Bonyan. [s3]

This example illustrates why integration does not necessarily mean that every function resides in one application. A specialist subsystem can have its own operational role while participating in a broader insurance environment. The supplier's claims about regulatory approvals have not been independently checked and should not be interpreted as a current authorization assessment. [s3]

content.heading: Implementation is part of the product
content.content:
Software delivery extends beyond installation. Fanavaran describes deployment work that includes assessing needs, planning projects, guiding users, resolving errors, testing, and releasing versions. It distinguishes implementation for a new insurance-company customer from adding products or subsystems for an existing customer. These descriptions show that insurance technology involves organizational change and continuing maintenance as well as software development. [s4]

Its support documentation separately describes teams organized around insurance business lines and teams organized around customers. It also identifies request-management systems and operational-server support. These are advertised service arrangements; no independently verified response-time or availability record was inspected. [s5]

For international readers, the supported conclusion is that Iran has a documented domestic insurance-software offering with multiple operational layers. A broader sector assessment still requires regulator publications, insurer-side evidence, and independent evaluation. Those sources are needed to explain how widely tools are deployed, how online distribution relates to underwriting, and whether automation improves outcomes.

name: Policy Management Systems
description: Policy management systems support the administration of insurance contracts and their connections to other insurer operations. Iranian supplier documentation provides a concrete example through Bonyan, while leaving deployment-specific performance and current supervisory requirements unverified.

seo.title: Insurance Policy Management Systems in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: A focused introduction to Iranian policy administration software, product rules, operational integration, and implementation evidence.

content.heading: The insurance contract as an operational record
content.content:
Policy management concerns the administration of insurance contracts within an insurer's working systems. An Iranian example is Bonyan, the core insurance platform described by Fanavaran, also known as IranEIT. Its product documentation groups policy issuance with claims, financial operations, and reinsurance, presenting contract administration as part of an integrated operational environment. This is a supplier's description of system scope rather than independent verification of a particular insurer's implementation. [s1]

The documentation lists insurance lines including vehicle, supplementary health, life, fire, cargo, liability, and engineering insurance. The breadth matters: a policy system must represent the products an insurer actually offers. A product catalogue on a vendor website nevertheless does not establish which modules each customer has deployed. [s1]

content.heading: Product rules and connected systems
content.content:
Bonyan's documentation identifies workflow capabilities and a rules engine, meaning software facilities for defining processes and applying business rules. It also advertises integration with SANHAB, identified there as Iran's central insurance monitoring and electronic supervision system. These statements describe intended capabilities; they do not disclose the precise reporting obligations, interface specifications, or configuration of an individual deployment. [s1]

Fanavaran's corporate history describes a further integration layer: an API-management infrastructure and interfaces for policy issuance and claims registration. That account links policy administration to services used by other software. It should not be read as confirmation that every interface is publicly accessible or that every insurer exposes the same operations. [s2]

content.heading: Making the system usable
content.content:
The practical work includes deciding how a product will operate in the customer's environment. Fanavaran's deployment description includes needs assessment, project design, user guidance, error resolution, testing, and version deployment. It distinguishes introducing its core platform to a new customer from installing additional subsystems or versions for an existing one. This makes implementation a continuing activity rather than a single installation event. [s3]

Support is another part of the documented operating model. The supplier describes both insurance-line specialists and customer-focused support teams, with requests recorded through interactive systems. Those arrangements identify channels for resolving business and technical questions; they do not establish actual resolution times or uninterrupted service. [s4]

content.heading: What the documentation establishes
content.content:
The available evidence supports a specific conclusion: a domestic Iranian supplier documents policy administration as a configurable, connected part of core insurance software. It does not support a ranking of policy platforms or claims that automation necessarily eliminates errors. Establishing those outcomes would require insurer-side records, documented test results, and independent operational evidence.

A fuller account also needs the rules and technical requirements applicable at the cutoff. Without those materials, advertised integration must remain distinct from verified compliance, and product scope must remain distinct from demonstrated deployment.
